title: Why trad jazz is neglected: universities and arts education
summary: Trad jazz panel without trad jazz; universities teach bebop; Wallace Davenport recalled a piano in every home.

bands.name: Art Blakey and the Jazz Messengers

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: Becoming a teacher: jazz in schools and conservatories

blocks.x: A couple of years ago I attended one of those jazz educator’s conferences, where thousands of people converge on the hotel, and I think it was in New York City. And they had a panel on traditional jazz. And they called it “Trad Jazz, Alive and Well” was the panel. But there was no trad jazz at the festival. They didn’t have any there. They didn’t have any bands performing it. And it was really odd.
Yeah. Right. Exactly. That says it all pretty much. It’s alive and well but where is it?

Well do you have an opinion on why trad jazz and New Orleans jazz and that, it’s so hard to define the stuff, but it doesn’t seem to be taken as seriously as John Coltrane, or Art Blakey and the Jazz Messengers. There seems to be —

Well I think, yeah, I think mainly right now the reason for that is because what’s promoted as — let’s see I’m trying to say this — the jazz that’s being taught at universities is more like bebop. And I don’t know that, and especially in America — I mean I think back to that whole value system for this music, be it whatever style of jazz, you just don’t have, our society doesn’t value it the way they did, I think, in the past, or as much, or maybe as many people, maybe that’s the better way to say it. And I think that’s as a result of a societal thing. Arts education is being cut in all the schools, and I mean when I was speaking to you earlier about Wallace Davenport, one of the older musicians that I started playing with when I was in the early years in New Orleans, and he played in Basie’s band and Hamp back then. But one of the things he told me one time, I remember him telling me about, he remembered the time when he was a young kid, everybody in New Orleans had a piano in their home. Well you know that doesn’t — © Fillius Jazz Archive -9-

so I mean there was some appreciation in every home, there was some appreciation of music. I mean people appreciated it, even if they weren’t going to be professional musicians, most people maybe had experiences with starting in a band program, or they could at least have some basic understanding to what it would take to become on the level that we know some of our greatest professional musicians are. And so you did have some appreciation there. But now it’s just all sports it seems. And I’m not knocking the football players, but I often think man, if we could just get somebody to go out and market music, market our music the way they market NBA basketball or NFL football. Then we’d be back. Or if there was a way to cross-market those things, then maybe we’d be back.
